Candidate data-generating processes

Unobserved-confounding policy-optimization study · discrete X (7 levels on [-1,1]), binary treatment. Explanations only: the model and its truth curves, no method results.

Each process draws a hidden confounder differently and induces a gap between the true treatment effect \(\tau(X)=\mathrm{E}[\mu_1-\mu_0\mid X]\) and the observed (confounded) contrast \(\mathrm{E}[Y\mid T{=}1,X]-\mathrm{E}[Y\mid T{=}0,X]\). The oracle treats where \(\tau(X)\gt 0\). Here \(\sigma\) is the logistic function. Idea 8 is a deliberate negative control (the confounder cancels in the contrast).

1. Binary hidden type (selection + outcome)

A hidden vitality type S that is more common at high fitness X dominates outcomes in both arms and also drives who is treated; the treatment helps the vital slightly more.

\[ S\in\{-1,+1\},\qquad \Pr(S{=}{+}1\mid X)=\sigma(8X), \] \[ e(X,S)=\sigma(0.8\,S-2X),\qquad \mu_0=5S,\quad \mu_1=6S+X, \] \[ \tau(X)=\mathbb{E}[\mu_1-\mu_0\mid X]=\big(2\sigma(8X)-1\big)+X. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

2. Continuous outcome confounder (Kallus style)

An unrecorded continuous prognosis U, correlated with X, raises outcomes in both arms and drives treatment; the confounder sits on the outcome as in Kallus and Zhou.

\[ U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(X,\,1),\qquad e=\sigma(U-1.5X), \] \[ \mu_0=4U,\qquad \mu_1=0.3\,X+4.5\,U, \] \[ \tau(X)=0.3X+(4.5-4)\,\mathbb{E}[U\mid X]=0.8\,X. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

3. X is a near-perfect proxy of U

The observed covariate X is a high-quality noisy measurement of the latent driver U, so balancing X almost fully balances the hidden U.

\[ U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(X,\,0.4^2),\qquad e=\sigma(1.2\,U-X), \] \[ \mu_0=4U,\qquad \mu_1=0.2\,X+4.6\,U,\qquad \tau(X)\approx 0.8\,X. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

4. Sign-flip effect modification (confounding by indication)

A hidden frailty flips the sign of the effect: the treatment helps the robust but harms the frail, and the frail are treated more, so the naive contrast points the wrong way (Simpson reversal).

\[ F\in\{0,1\},\qquad \Pr(F{=}1\mid X)=\sigma(-5X),\qquad e=\sigma(1.2\,F-X), \] \[ \mu_0=-3F,\qquad \mu_1=\mu_0+\big(\mathbf{1}[F{=}0]\,(+2)+\mathbf{1}[F{=}1]\,(-2)\big), \] \[ \tau(X)=2\big(1-\Pr(F{=}1\mid X)\big)-2\,\Pr(F{=}1\mid X). \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

5. Multiplicative confounding (hidden U scales the effect)

A hidden positive vitality factor U multiplies the treatment benefit, so the same intervention helps high-U patients far more; U also confounds the baseline.

\[ \log U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(0.8X,\,0.5^2),\qquad e=\sigma(\log U-X), \] \[ \mu_0=U,\qquad \mu_1=\mu_0+(-0.2+X)\,U, \] \[ \tau(X)=(-0.2+X)\,\mathbb{E}[U\mid X]. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

6. Saturating dose-response with a treatment cost

Outcomes are a saturating function of a latent health index; the treatment shifts the index but costs a fixed amount, so it is only worth it on the steep part of the curve.

\[ U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(X,\,1),\qquad \eta=X+U,\qquad e=\sigma(U-0.5X), \] \[ \mu_0=4\,\sigma(2\eta),\qquad \mu_1=4\,\sigma\!\big(2(\eta+1.2)\big)-0.5, \] \[ \tau(X)=\mathbb{E}\big[\mu_1-\mu_0\mid X\big]. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

7. Latent class mixture (responders vs non-responders)

A hidden subgroup determines the benefit: responders (more likely at high X) gain a lot, non-responders little or nothing, and responders also have a better baseline.

\[ R\in\{0,1\},\qquad \Pr(R{=}1\mid X)=\sigma(4X),\qquad e=\sigma(1.2\,R), \] \[ \mu_0=2R,\qquad \mu_1=\mu_0+\big(\mathbf{1}[R{=}1]\,(2.5)+\mathbf{1}[R{=}0]\,(-0.5)\big), \] \[ \tau(X)=2.5\,\Pr(R{=}1\mid X)-0.5\big(1-\Pr(R{=}1\mid X)\big). \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

8. Cancelling baseline (negative control)

The hidden U shifts the baseline equally in both arms, so it CANCELS in the treat-minus-control contrast and the true effect is a clean function of X. Included to show where O-W has nothing to add.

\[ U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(X,\,1),\qquad e=\sigma(U-X), \] \[ \mu_0=4U,\qquad \mu_1=\mu_0+0.8\,X, \] \[ \tau(X)=0.8\,X\quad(\text{U cancels in the contrast}). \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

9. Two correlated hidden confounders

Selection is driven by one latent variable while outcomes are driven by another, correlated one, so no single observed proxy explains assignment, yet the prognosis confounder still tracks X.

\[ U_1=0.8X+Z_1,\quad U_2=0.8X+0.7\,Z_1+\sqrt{1-0.7^2}\,Z_2,\quad Z_1,Z_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), \] \[ e=\sigma(U_1-X),\qquad \mu_0=4\,U_2,\qquad \mu_1=0.3X+4.4\,U_2, \] \[ \tau(X)=0.3X+(4.4-4)\,\mathbb{E}[U_2\mid X]. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.

10. Interaction in the treated arm only (clean control)

The control outcome depends only on observed X, but the treatment effect depends on a hidden fitness U that also drives treatment, so the treated arm alone is confounded.

\[ U\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(0.5X,\,1),\qquad e=\sigma(U-X), \] \[ \mu_0=0,\qquad \mu_1=(-0.3+0.3X)+4\,U, \] \[ \tau(X)=(-0.3+0.3X)+4\cdot 0.5\,X. \]

The shaded band marks the X levels the oracle treats. Where the grey dashed observed contrast departs from the black true effect, unobserved confounding is biasing the naive estimate.
